newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Conflict spreads in east Zaire, U.N. pulls out.
newsitem.headline: Conflict spreads in east Zaire, U.N. pulls out.

text.p: The United Nations pulled its aid workers out of eastern Zaire on Saturday after conflict pitting Tutsi rebels against Zairean troops threatened to engulf much of the region.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali earlier called for an emergency mission to go to Zaire followed by an international conference to prevent warfare spreading throughout central Africa.

Two U.N. planes evacuated a total of 128 U.N. and other expatriate aid workers and some other foreigners from the eastern Zairean town of Bukavu and headed for Uganda, said U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) spokeswoman Brenda Barton in Nairobi.
The rebels were reported to have captured two towns in the east of the country, to have panicked 200,000 Rwandans into fleeing the second biggest refugee camp in Zaire and to have wounded 50.
A string of camps in Zaire houses 1.1. million Rwandan refugees, including perpetrators of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda in which Hutus killed up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
In total, nearly half-a-million refugees are now estimated to be on the move as a result of Tutsi rebel tactics.
Both Rwanda and Burundi, Zaire's small neighbours to the east, are governed by Tutsi ethnic minorities and diplomats fear they could be drawn into the conflict.
Military sources and state radio in Burundi said the town of Uvira at the northern end of Lake Tanganyika had fallen to the rebels after two days of battles with Zairean forces.
Aid workers in Goma, eastern Zaire, and in Geneva said Tutsi fighters had also captured the town of Rutshuru 50 km (30 miles) from Goma city, the capital of North Kivu province.

For the first time, large numbers of Rwandan refugees were reported to be on the move in the Goma region north of here. Rutshuru is only 10 km (six miles) away from sprawling camps home to 700,000 Hutus.
Aid workers said one camp, Kibumba, a virtual city of about 200,000 people complete with restaurants, bars, shops and hotels, had emptied of refugees in the space of hours.

"Kibumba camp is completely empty and smoke is rising from the area. Many thousands are moving westwards...there are no volunteers to repatriate to Rwanda," said Paul Stromberg, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
Nearly 300,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees were uprooted from camps in South Kivu province by fighting in the past week.
Aid officials said the latest exodus of refugees had been triggered by shooting in the Kibumba camp.
Stromberg said by telephone from the Rwanda capital Kigali at least 50 wounded arrived at Goma hospital after the shooting.

Elodie Martel, head of the Goma delegation of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), said the attackers appeared to be the same group as Tutsi rebels who advanced against Zairean troops in South Kivu.
Other aid officials said large explosions, apparently mortar bombs, were heard in or around Kibumba on Friday and Saturday.

In Bukavu, 100 km (60 miles) to the north of Uvira, four mortar blasts on Saturday morning rocked the area of the Panzi camp, home to some 2,000 former Hutu soldiers, veterans of the Rwandan civil war, and 5,000 members of their families.
After the explosions, refugees, many on crutches and in wheelchairs, streamed out of the camp.
Bukavu was tense and Zairean soldiers, who have repeatedly harassed journalists, on Saturday robbed at gunpoint two reporters travelling in a car in the city.
The soldiers prodded a machine-gun into the stomach of Reuters Television cameraman Marc Hoogsteyns and put a hand grenade in his mouth before escaping with many of his belongings.
Martin Dawes of the British Broadcasting Corporation was also robbed by the group of about six soldiers.
The Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels say they are fighting Zairean troops after a Zairean order to expel them from the country.
The Banyamulenge arrived in the region up to 200 years ago but ethnic tensions have become acute in the aftermath of the 1994 genocide and civil war in Rwanda.
Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko has been absent from the country for more than two months, receiving cancer treatment in Switzerland, and his long illness is fuelling the crisis.
